WorkSmart-AI · Copilot curriculum

Copilot in plain English

Every term you will hear in a Copilot session, explained once, without the marketing. Written for the person using it, not the person configuring it.

Search or filter below. The tag on each entry says which part of the picture it belongs to.

If you only learn four

Agent
Who does the work — a named Copilot with a job, rules, and a fixed set of places it may read.
Skill
What that agent can do — one named task, described once and reused.
Action
What it can reach — the ability to touch a real system: read a library, send a mail, update a list.
Workflow
When, and in what order — steps that fire on a trigger and run without you sitting there.

A

Action

Building

An agent’s ability to touch a real system rather than just talk about it — read a document library, send an email, add a row to a list, create a task. Without actions, an agent can only produce text.

Also called a tool, or a connector, depending on which screen you are looking at.

Agent

Building

A Copilot you have given a name, a job, a set of rules and a fixed set of sources. Instead of explaining the task every time, you explain it once and then talk to the thing you made. Colleagues can use it too.

Not the same as Agent Mode, which is ordinary Copilot working harder inside one document.

Agent Mode

Surfaces

Copilot taking on a whole multi-step job inside Word, Excel or PowerPoint — building a document or reworking a spreadsheet across several moves — rather than making one edit and stopping.

Agent Store

Building

Where ready-made agents are published — Microsoft’s, your organisation’s, and third parties’. Worth a look before you build anything: somebody has often done it already.

Analyst

Building

A specialist agent that works with data. Give it a spreadsheet or a set of figures and it reasons through the analysis, writes and runs the code, and shows you its working.

Approval step

Building

A point in a workflow where a person has to say yes before anything continues. The safety catch on automation, and usually the difference between a workflow you can defend and one you cannot.

Also called human in the loop.

Audit trail

Trust

The record of what Copilot was asked and what it did, kept by your organisation. It exists, and it matters for FOI, data-protection requests and investigations.

Autonomy

Building

Whether an agent waits to be asked or acts on its own. Most agents you meet are the first kind. The second kind needs an owner, a scope, and someone who checks on it.

C

Commercial data protection

Trust

The promise that what you type at work stays inside your organisation’s boundary and is not used to train the public model. It applies when you are signed in with your work account — which is the whole reason to use the work version rather than a personal one.

Connector

Work IQ

A bridge that lets Copilot read a system that is not Microsoft’s — a student record system, a CRM, a ticketing tool. Someone in IT sets these up; you only notice that Copilot suddenly knows more.

Consumption and credits

Trust

Agent runs cost money, metered per run rather than covered by a flat licence. Relevant the moment you build something that runs on a schedule rather than when you press a button.

Copilot Academy

Licence

Guided Copilot training already switched on inside Viva Learning for most Microsoft 365 users. Free, already paid for, and usually nobody knows it is there.

Copilot Actions

Surfaces

Copilot carrying out a task on your device or in the browser on your behalf — filling a form, working through a website — rather than telling you how to do it.

Not the same as an action in the agent sense, which is a capability you grant an agent you built.

Copilot Chat

Licence

The free tier, included with a work sign-in. Protected, useful, and grounded in the web — but it cannot see your files, mail or meetings unless you paste them in.

Copilot Notebooks

Surfaces

A place to pin the sources for one project — a set of documents, pages and notes — so that every question you ask is answered from those, and only those. The fix for “it keeps dragging in the wrong report”.

Copilot Pages

Surfaces

Turns an answer in a chat into a document you and colleagues can edit together. Use it the moment an answer is worth keeping; chat threads are disposable, pages are not.

Copilot Premium

Licence

The top tier. Adds the specialist reasoning agents, the ability to build agents, and higher usage limits, on top of everything the standard licence gives you.

Copilot Search

Surfaces

Search across your organisation’s content that answers the question rather than handing you twenty links to open.

Copilot Studio

Building

The place where agents are built, tested and published — without writing code. This is where a repeated prompt becomes something your team can use.

Not the same as Power Automate, which follows fixed rules. Studio builds something that exercises judgement.

Custom instructions

Asking

Standing context you set once — your role, your department, how you like things written — so you stop retyping it in every prompt.

Custom-engine agent

Building

An agent built from scratch by developers rather than configured on top of Copilot. Worth knowing the phrase exists so you can recognise when a conversation has left your territory.

D

Declarative agent

Building

The ordinary kind — an agent you make by describing what it should do and which sources it may use. Everything a business user builds is one of these.

Deep reasoning

Building

Copilot taking longer to think before it answers. Slower and more expensive, and worth it for genuine analysis rather than for drafting an email.

DLP

Trust

Data loss prevention — the rules your organisation sets about what can leave, and where. Copilot obeys them, which is occasionally why an answer stops short.

G

Grounding

Work IQ

Answering from real sources rather than from memory. A grounded answer can cite where it came from; an ungrounded one is the model’s best guess. Always check which you were given.

H

Hallucination

Asking

A confident, fluent, wrong answer. It is not a bug being fixed next release — it is how these tools work, and it is why verification is your job rather than Microsoft’s.

Human in the loop

Building

See Approval step.

I

Instructions

Building

What you write when you build an agent: its job, its rules, its tone, what it must never do. The single biggest lever on whether the agent is any good.

Iteration

Asking

Steering the answer with follow-up turns instead of retyping the prompt from scratch. “Shorter.” “More formal.” “Now for the student audience.” The cheapest skill on this list and the most under-used.

K

Knowledge source

Work IQ

The specific places an agent is allowed to read — a SharePoint site, a set of documents, a connector. Narrowing these is what turns a vague agent into a reliable one.

M

Memory

Work IQ

Copilot holding on to preferences and context across sessions, so it does not start from nothing each morning. Check what it has remembered occasionally; it is editable.

Microsoft Graph

Work IQ

The plumbing underneath Work IQ — the layer that holds your files, mail, calendar, chats and the connections between people. You will hear it named in IT conversations and never need to touch it.

Microsoft 365 Copilot

Licence

The paid seat. This is the one that can see your work — files, mail, chats, meetings — and that appears inside Word, Excel, Outlook and Teams.

Not the same as Copilot Chat, which is free and cannot reach your work data.

Multi-agent orchestration

Building

Agents handing work to other agents. Real, occasionally useful, and firmly a job for whoever owns the platform rather than for you on a Tuesday afternoon.

O

Oversharing

Trust

Copilot surfacing something that was always technically visible to you but practically buried — an old pay file in a site nobody tidied. Copilot did not break a permission. It found one that was already wrong.

P

Permissions inheritance

Trust

Copilot can only see what your account can already see — no more, and no less. The answer to “can it read my colleague’s mail?” is no, unless you already could.

Prompt

Asking

What you ask for. A good one carries five things: the goal, the context, the sourceto use, the format you want back, and the tone. Most disappointing answers are missing three of those.

Prompt Gallery

Asking

A library of prompts inside Copilot — Microsoft’s, your organisation’s, and ones you save yourself. Start here rather than from a blank box.

R

Referencing

Asking

Pointing Copilot at a specific file, person or meeting inside your prompt, usually by typing a slash or an oblique. Turns “summarise our policy” into a question it can actually answer.

Researcher

Building

A specialist agent that works through a question over several steps, across your work data and the web, and comes back with a sourced report rather than a paragraph.

Responsible use

Trust

Your institution’s own rules about what AI may be used for — marking, admissions, personal data, student-facing decisions. These sit above anything Microsoft permits, and they are the ones you will be held to.

S

Saved and team prompts

Asking

A prompt you keep, and one your team shares. The step between “I worked out a good prompt” and “the department has a good prompt”.

Sensitivity label

Trust

The classification stuck to a document — public, internal, confidential. Copilot respects it and passes it on to anything it produces from that document.

SharePoint agent

Building

An agent created straight from a document library, so it answers only from what is in there. The easiest first agent anyone builds, and often the only one a team needs.

Skill

Building

One named thing an agent can do, written out once: “triage an enquiry”, “draft a reply in our house style”, “flag anything about fees”. An agent with three clear skills beats an agent with one vague instruction.

Not the same as a workflow. A skill sits ready to be used; a workflow is an order of events that fires on its own.

T

Tacit knowledge

Adoption

What your team knows but has never written down — so Copilot cannot read it. The most common reason a technically correct answer is still the wrong answer for your institution.

Tenant

Trust

Your organisation’s own walled section of Microsoft’s cloud. “Inside the tenant” means inside the boundary your data protection promise covers.

Trigger

Building

What starts a workflow without you: a time of day, an email arriving, a file being added, a form being submitted. Choosing the trigger is most of designing the workflow.

U

Use case

Adoption

A specific job in your actual week that Copilot could take on. Not “improve productivity” — “turn Monday’s three committee papers into a one-page brief before Tuesday”.

V

Verification

Asking

Checking the output before you use it. This does not transfer to the tool, the vendor or your IT department. If it goes out under your name, it is yours.

W

Work, web, or both

Asking

The toggle that decides whether Copilot answers from your organisation’s content, from the open internet, or from both. It changes the answer completely, and people forget it is there.

Work IQ

Work IQ

The layer that gives Copilot an understanding of your organisation — your documents, mail, meetings, and how people and projects connect. It is the reason Copilot’s answer is different from a public chatbot’s, and the reason it can be wrong in specific, local ways.

What it is not: a person reading your email. It is a permissions-bound index your account already had access to.

Workflow

Building

An ordered set of steps that runs on a trigger, usually without you watching. A step can call an agent, wait for a person to approve, and then carry on.

Not the same as an agent. The agent is the worker; the workflow is the rota.

Nothing matches that. Try a shorter word, or clear the filter.

A note on names. Microsoft renames things often. The four core terms — agent, skill, action, workflow — describe how the thing works and will outlast whatever it is called this quarter. If a name here does not match what is on your screen, trust the screen and tell us, and we will update this page.
